item.title: NVIDIA Extends DGX Spark Edge AI with TensorRT Edge-LLM and Nemotron-3.5 Lightning
item.description:
NVIDIA Extends DGX Spark Edge AI with TensorRT Edge-LLM and Nemotron-3.5 Lightning

AI workloads are moving beyond the data center. Developers are building agents that run at the edge—monitoring driver attention, helping robots navigate, and coordinating production‑line fleets. These applications must operate within tight memory, power, and latency budgets. NVIDIA now offers the DGX Spark platform in a 64 GB configuration together with the TensorRT Edge‑LLM runtime, enabling developers to prototype, fine‑tune, and test large‑language models such as Nemotron‑3.5 Lightning directly on edge hardware.

🔍 Overview

  • Physical AI agents need compact, low‑latency inference.
  • DGX Spark 64 GB provides the compute and memory headroom for edge prototyping.
  • TensorRT Edge‑LLM delivers a lightweight C++ inference runtime for embedded targets (Jetson Thor, DRIVE AGX Thor, IGX Thor).

🧩 How it works

  • The trtedge command‑line interface (CLI) downloads the selected model (≈21 GB) and builds TensorRT engines optimized for the Spark platform.
  • Once built, engines are cached in ~/.cache/tensorrt-edgellm and reused on later launches.
  • A local OpenAI‑compatible API server can host the model, confirming readiness with a "status":"ready" JSON response.
  • DSpark speculative decoding can be enabled: a draft model proposes several tokens, which the main model validates in a single pass, reducing generation latency.

⚙️ Key details

  • Required software stack: NVIDIA CUDA 13, TensorRT 10.16.1.11 or newer (10.x series), Python 3.10‑3.12.
  • Tested versions: TensorRT Edge‑LLM 0.11.1 and TensorRT 10.16.1.11.
  • Use a Python virtual environment to keep newly installed packages separate while still accessing system‑wide TensorRT libraries.
  • Verify the TensorRT version with the provided check command; if bindings are missing, install the compatible TensorRT 10.x package via the NVIDIA TensorRT pip instructions.
  • First launch downloads the model and builds the engine; subsequent launches reuse cached engines, accelerating startup.

🚀 Performance

  • TensorRT Edge‑LLM with Nemotron‑3.5 Lightning yields low response latency and fast token generation on DGX Spark 64 GB.
  • DSpark speculative decoding (using three draft tokens) improves generation speed; the exact time‑to‑first‑token (TTFT) and token‑per‑second rates are reported in the reference table.
  • Users can tune num_speculative_tokens and other settings to balance speed and accuracy for their workload.

📦 Availability

  • DGX Spark 64 GB configuration is now available for embedded developers.
  • TensorRT Edge‑LLM is released with support for the same inference framework on development (Spark) and deployment platforms such as NVIDIA Jetson Thor, NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor, and NVIDIA IGX Thor.
  • The tutorial demonstrates running the text‑only Nemotron‑3.5 Lightning model on Spark and enabling DSpark speculative decoding.

#NVIDIA #EdgeAI #TensorRT #LLM

Source: Run AI Models for Edge Application Development with Just a Few Commands | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: Exowatt Deploys Edge AI Agents for Solar‑Powered Data Center Alarm Triage
item.description:
Exowatt Deploys Edge AI Agents for Solar‑Powered Data Center Alarm Triage

Exowatt has expanded its modular, dispatchable solar platform with AI agents that autonomously triage alarms and perform energy‑market analysis, using a serverless model‑customization pipeline on AWS.

🔍 Overview

  • Exowatt builds modular, dispatchable solar systems for energy‑intensive applications such as AI data centers.
  • The flagship Exowatt P3 captures solar energy with optical lenses, stores it as heat in a long‑duration thermal battery, and dispatches electricity on demand via a heat engine.
  • P3 powers data centers directly behind the meter, avoiding multi‑year grid interconnection queues.
  • A fleet of AI agents monitors live alarms at the edge, where connectivity may be limited or absent.
  • The AI pipeline now turns raw operational data into a certified training set, a fine‑tuned model, and a deployed artifact in days rather than months.

🧩 How it works

Solar system

  • Optical lenses concentrate sunlight onto a thermal absorber.
  • Heat is stored in a thermal battery for long‑duration discharge.
  • A heat engine converts stored heat to electricity on demand.

AI pipeline

  • Raw alarm and market data are collected from each site.
  • Open‑weight base models are fine‑tuned with Low‑Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and supervised fine‑tuning (SFT) on Amazon SageMaker AI.
  • Serverless training allocates capacity on demand, allowing multiple experiments per day.
  • The best model is registered in the SageMaker AI Model Registry and hosted via Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import.
  • Edge‑deployed models run on no‑GPU controllers; cloud‑deployed models run in the Cloud EMS.

AWS services powering the pipeline

Service Role
Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import Hosts the fine‑tuned Qwen3‑14B for Cloud EMS (private invocation)
Amazon Bedrock (Qwen3‑VL‑235B) Provides paraphrasing for alarm‑triage
Amazon Bedrock (Claude Sonnet 4.6) Provides paraphrasing for energy‑market analysis
Amazon SageMaker AI (serverless model customization) Fine‑tunes open‑weight base models using LoRA and SFT
Amazon SageMaker AI Model Registry Stores and versions the evaluated deployment artifact

⚙️ Key details

  • Edge alarm‑triage uses the Qwen3‑1.7B model, fine‑tuned for the specific hardware and logic of Exowatt’s EMS.
  • Cloud energy‑market analysis uses the larger Qwen3‑14B model.
  • The fine‑tuned models achieve higher accuracy than frontier models at up to 49× lower cost.
  • Models are small enough to run on edge controllers without GPUs yet accurate enough for autonomous operation.
  • The pipeline can be reused to build smaller, task‑specific models across the growing fleet of sites.

💡 Why it matters

  • Enables data centers to come online quickly without waiting for grid interconnection.
  • Provides reliable alarm monitoring even when connectivity is intermittent.
  • Reduces operational cost by avoiding per‑decision calls to large frontier models.
  • Accelerates model development from months to days, supporting rapid deployment as the fleet scales toward thousands of units.

#Exowatt #AIagents #SolarPower #AWS #EdgeAI

Source: Exowatt beats frontier models on accuracy with SageMaker serverless model customization | Amazon Web Services

item.title: LFM3 Unifies Text, Vision, Audio, Omni, and Decision Models on a 2‑Billion‑Parameter Backbone
item.description:
LFM3 Unifies Text, Vision, Audio, Omni, and Decision Models on a 2‑Billion‑Parameter Backbone

The latest release, LFM3, is the new generation of Liquid Foundation Models that unifies text, vision, audio, omni, and decision capabilities on a shared ~2 B‑parameter backbone.

🔍 Overview

  • LFM3 is built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence.
  • It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, each in the ~2 B‑parameter range.
  • Every modality model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base.

🧩 How it works

  • Tri‑hybrid architecture: 13 gated short convolutions (kernel size 7), 5 sliding‑window attention layers with a 256‑token window, and 6 global attention layers.
  • Head‑wise gated attention: a sigmoid gate scales each head’s output, allowing a head to switch off when it adds nothing.
  • Partial RoPE: global attention layers rotate only the highest‑frequency half of each head, keeping the other half invariant to distance.
  • Hardware‑in‑the‑loop architecture search redesigns the model for agentic use cases and now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs/GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Parameter efficiency: LFM3‑1.7B outperforms LFM2.5‑2.6B while using 35 % fewer parameters.
  • Speed: With an 8 K‑token context it is about 25 % faster per parameter than LFM2‑1.2B on edge devices.
  • Context window: The text model supports a 256 K‑token window; the final 3.5 T pre‑training tokens extend this window.
  • Pre‑training: 22 T tokens using the same 128 K vocabulary as LFM2.5‑8B‑A1B, with the last 3.5 T tokens emphasizing agentic traces and tool calls.
  • Edge readiness:
    • Text model fits in ~1 GB at 4‑bit precision.
    • Vision encoder combines convolution and attention, using 3× less compute than the SigLIP2 encoder in previous LFM VL models.
    • The 164 M‑parameter vision encoder matches Qwen3.5‑2B’s vision accuracy while requiring 2.2× fewer FLOPs.
    • LiquidCodec audio tokenizer turns generated tokens into speech at ~87× real‑time on a single CPU thread on Apple M4 Max and supports streaming decoding.
  • Fine‑tuning: Any modality model can be fine‑tuned on a single GPU and deployed where the application runs.

Model variants (all derived from LFM3‑1.7B‑Base)

Variant Modality Notable features
Text Text ~1 GB at 4‑bit, 256 K context window, suitable for on‑device agents
Vision Vision Convolution + attention, 3× less compute than SigLIP2, matches Qwen3.5‑2B accuracy with 2.2× fewer FLOPs
Audio Audio Uses LiquidCodec tokenizer, ~87× real‑time speech generation on Apple M4 Max, streaming decoding
Omni Omni First omni model sharing the same backbone
Decision Decision Shares backbone, optimized for agentic tasks

🚀 Availability

  • Models can be fine‑tuned on a single GPU and deployed on the target hardware, including phones, Raspberry Pi 5, laptops, cloud CPUs/GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.
  • Recommended for local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or as a base for domain‑specific fine‑tuning.

💡 Why it matters

  • The shared backbone provides more capability per parameter, allowing a 1.7 B‑parameter model to outperform larger predecessors.
  • Unified architecture across modalities reduces the need for separate model families.
  • Edge‑centric design—small size, fast inference, long context—enables advanced agentic tasks to run locally without cloud dependence.

#LiquidFoundationModels #MultimodalAI #EdgeAI #ModelOptimization

Source: Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

item.title: LFM2.5-24B-A2B: A Fast On-Device MoE Reasoning Model for Agentic Tasks
item.description:
LFM2.5-24B-A2B: A Fast On-Device MoE Reasoning Model for Agentic Tasks

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a new reasoning-only model designed for fast, private agentic workflows on-device. Building upon the LFM2-24B-A2B architecture, this update introduces scaled training, expanded context windows, and explicit chain-of-thought reasoning to provide competitive performance against significantly larger models.

🔍 Overview

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a Mixture of Experts (MoE) model that always produces an explicit chain of thought before providing a final answer. While it is the smallest model in its evaluation group, it is competitive with models like Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, which has ~50% more total and active parameters. Its primary strengths are tool use and instruction following.

🧩 How it works

The model retains its predecessor’s architecture while scaling training and context capabilities:

  • Architecture: 40 layers with 64 experts per MoE block and top-4 routing.
  • Hybrid Design: Uses a combination of gated short convolutions and Grouped Query Attention (GQA).
  • Training Scale: Pre-training was scaled from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training added 2.3T tokens across 32K and 131K context lengths, emphasizing reasoning, math, and long-context data.
  • Tokenizer: An in-place expansion doubled the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for improved non-Latin tokenization.

⚙️ Key details

Feature Specification
Total Parameters 24 Billion
Active Parameters 2 Billion per token
Context Window 131,000 tokens
Vocabulary Size 128,000 tokens

In benchmark testing, the model leads or matches competition on five of eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks. On LiveClaw, it scored 48.09 compared to 38.19 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. On AutomationBench, it scored more than three times the next-best model.

🚀 Availability

LFM2.5-24B-A2B includes day-one support for several inference ecosystems:

  • llama.cpp
  • MLX
  • vLLM
  • SGLang
  • ONNX

💡 Why it matters

This model is optimized for high-speed edge and GPU inference. It decodes at 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395, making it up to 1.7x faster than the next-best compared model while using the least memory. On a single NVIDIA B300 GPU, it can reach over 21,000 output tokens per second. For knowledge-heavy workloads, users are encouraged to pair the model with retrieval or web search, as larger models maintain an edge on benchmarks like GPQA Diamond and SWE-Bench.

#AIagents #EdgeAI #MoE #LiquidFoundationModel

Source: Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

item.title: Microsoft and Nvidia Unveil Surface Laptop Ultra for Local AI Processing
item.description:
Microsoft and Nvidia Unveil Surface Laptop Ultra for Local AI Processing

Microsoft and Nvidia have introduced the Surface Laptop Ultra, a high-performance Windows computer designed to run sophisticated AI models directly on the device. This development is part of a broader strategy to distribute AI workloads between local hardware and cloud infrastructure to improve privacy and reduce operating costs.

🔍 Overview

The Surface Laptop Ultra is engineered to process AI tasks locally, moving away from a total reliance on remote cloud servers. This approach allows businesses to maintain greater control over sensitive information while enabling advanced models to operate efficiently on personal hardware.

🧩 How it works

Microsoft’s strategy involves dividing AI tasks to optimize performance and security:

  • Hybrid Workloads: AI tasks are split between the local device and cloud infrastructure to balance cost and privacy.
  • Local Execution: High-performance configurations allow models to run directly on the hardware, reducing the need for constant cloud connectivity.
  • Secure Environment: The system uses specialized containers to isolate AI activities from unauthorized data access.

⚙️ Key details

The hardware and software integration includes several specific technologies aimed at performance and safety:

  • Nvidia RTX Spark: The core technology powering the device’s high-performance AI capabilities.
  • Microsoft Execution Containers: A security system designed to prevent AI agents from accessing unauthorized information or performing actions outside of permitted boundaries.

🚀 Availability

The Surface Laptop Ultra is available at different price points depending on the configuration:

Configuration Price
Starting Price $2,599
High-Performance Configurations Up to $5,899

💡 Why it matters

As companies spend extraordinary sums on AI development, investors and governments are increasingly seeking evidence that these investments can deliver sustainable returns without creating unacceptable risks. This local processing shift addresses these concerns by potentially reducing cloud costs and enhancing privacy. These security features arrive as a new national survey found that nearly two-thirds of Americans believe AI is developing too quickly.

#Microsoft #Nvidia #EdgeAI #Surface #Cybersecurity

Source: Top AI News Stories This Week (October 5–9, 2026)

item.title: EmbeddingGemma 2 Brings Unified Multimodal Embeddings to On‑Device AI
item.description:
EmbeddingGemma 2 Brings Unified Multimodal Embeddings to On‑Device AI

🔍 Overview

  • Today we are launching EmbeddingGemma 2, a unified multimodal embedding model that expands beyond text to include code, images, video, and audio.
  • Built on the Gemma 4 architecture and released under the Apache 2.0 license, the model has 740 million parameters and is optimized for on‑device inference.

🧩 How it works

  • EmbeddingGemma 2 shares the same text tokenizer and audio encoder as Gemma 4, allowing the two models to run together in a single pipeline with a lower combined memory footprint.
  • The model uses Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) so output vectors can be truncated from 768 dimensions down to 512, 256, or 128 dimensions, giving up to 6× storage reduction for local vector databases.

⚙️ Key details

  • Multimodal capabilities – a single model can locate a specific video clip from a voice memo or search hours of audio recordings with a text query.
  • Benchmark performance – achieves leading scores among sub‑1B multimodal embedders on benchmarks such as MTEB Code and MAEB, and matches or outperforms many larger models on text, vision, and audio tasks.
  • Code improvement – code performance jumps 9.92 points on MTEB Code (68.76 → 78.68), making it suitable for local codebase indexing and semantic code search.
  • Modular size options
    Variant Parameters
    Text‑only 270 M
    Vision encoder (optional) 170 M
    Audio encoder (optional) 300 M
  • Extended context – 8 K token window (4× larger than EmbeddingGemma 1), enabling processing of up to 5.5 minutes of audio, 29 images, 58 video frames, or interleaved combinations on local hardware.
  • On‑device efficiency – with quantization, a Google Pixel 11 Pro uses ~191 MB active RAM for text‑only weights and ~567 MB for the full multimodal model.
  • Quality‑per‑parameter – sets a new standard for sub‑1B models across image, video, document, and audio tasks, even outperforming specialist models more than twice its size.

🚀 Availability

  • Model weights are available on Hugging Face and Kaggle; Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Model Garden will add the model soon.
  • Optimized versions can be found in the LiteRT Community on Hugging Face.
  • Deploy on edge hardware with Google AI Edge MediaPipe (turnkey embedding, retrieval & decision) or LiteRT for custom integration.
  • Build for browsers using transformers.js or WebGPU.
  • Supported runtimes include transformers, sentence‑transformers, MLX, vLLM, llama.cpp, SGLang, Ollama, LMStudio.
  • Store embedding vectors with Qdrant.
  • Fine‑tuning guidance is provided by Unsloth.

💡 Why it matters

  • Generating embeddings locally guarantees data privacy and reduces pipeline latency.
  • Enables fully offline, cross‑modal search and retrieval, empowering developers to build on‑device RAG pipelines that understand complex multimodal data when paired with generative models such as Gemma 4.
  • The developer community’s response to the original EmbeddingGemma exceeded expectations, with more than 20 million downloads used for smarter on‑device search tools and privacy‑first RAG pipelines.

#EmbeddingGemma #MultimodalAI #EdgeAI

Source: EmbeddingGemma 2: an open, lightweight multimodal embedding model

item.title: Offline Voice-First AI Stack Benchmarked on Jetson Orin and Raspberry Pi5
item.description:
Offline Voice-First AI Stack Benchmarked on Jetson Orin and Raspberry Pi5

A new workstream titled Offline AI Modules: Voice-First Offline Architecture, Hardware Reference Stack, Quantization and Benchmarking was submitted on 4 Oct 2026. It delivers a practical, low‑power, community‑accessible solution for voice‑first AI systems that run fully offline.

🔍 Overview

  • Targets African language communities where speech is the dominant interaction mode and internet connectivity is unreliable or absent.
  • Provides three reinforcing components:
    • A modular voice‑first offline architecture.
    • A low‑cost hardware reference bill of materials.
    • A reproducible quantization and benchmarking pipeline for instruction‑tuned language models in the 2‑5 B parameter class.

🧩 How it works

  • The stack is evaluated end‑to‑end across two hardware tiers:
    • Tier B: NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX.
    • Tier A: Raspberry Pi 5.
  • Three instruction‑tuned models are run through four quantization formats.
  • Evaluation metrics include decode throughput, chat latency, memory usage, power consumption, multilingual topic‑classification accuracy (MasakhaNEWS in English, Hausa, Igbo, Nigerian Pidgin, Yoruba), per‑language perplexity drift, and speech‑recognition performance (Ethio‑ASR on Amharic and Oromo).

⚙️ Key details

  • Best trade‑off: Q4_K_M quantization.
  • Performance on Tier B (Jetson Orin NX):
    • Model gemma‑4‑E2B‑it achieves 28.8 t/s decode throughput and 89.2 % topic classification accuracy at Q4_K_M.
  • Performance on Tier A (Raspberry Pi 5):
    • All three models run within a 16 GB memory budget.
Tier Hardware Decode Throughput (t/s) Topic Classification Accuracy Memory Budget
B NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX 28.8 (gemma‑4‑E2B‑it, Q4_K_M) 89.2 % (Q4_K_M) —
A Raspberry Pi 5 — — 16 GB (all models)

🚀 Availability

  • The full paper and benchmark results are available as of the 4 Oct 2026 submission.

💡 Why it matters

  • Enables offline, low‑power voice AI for regions with limited connectivity.
  • Supports a range of African languages, expanding access to speech‑driven technology.
  • Provides a reproducible pipeline that can be adopted by the broader community for similar deployments.

#OfflineAI #VoiceFirst #EdgeAI #AfricanLanguages

Source: Offline AI Modules: Voice-First Offline Architecture, Hardware Reference Stack, Quantization and Benchmarking Source: EMODE: Dynamic Para-Semantic Experts for Emotion-Aware Speech Language Modeling Source: AccentCL: Robust Accent Classification with Incremental Expansion Source: Quality-Aware Self-Correcting Speech Translation on an Edge Device

item.title: Sightlogix Launches NS12 and TC12 Megapixel Thermal Cameras for Large Scale Perimeter Security
item.description:
Sightlogix Launches NS12 and TC12 Megapixel Thermal Cameras for Large Scale Perimeter Security

Sightlogix has announced the Sightsensor NS12 and TC12, which are among the first fixed thermal cameras on the market to feature a 1280×1024 imager. These devices are designed to protect large sites and critical infrastructure perimeters using high-resolution thermal imaging and edge-based AI classification.

🔍 Overview

The higher resolution of the NS12 and TC12 allows each camera to protect approximately 2.5 times the area of a traditional 640×480 system. By increasing coverage per device, the system reduces the total infrastructure cost for wide-area sites.

  • Target Applications: Utility substations, data centres, airports, ports, and wide-area campuses.
  • Infrastructure Impact: Fewer cameras require fewer poles and fewer cable runs.
  • Detection Range: Both cameras deliver AI classification across the full inbound detection range.

🧩 How it works

The cameras are powered by the Sightlogix Gen7 edge processing platform, which includes a dedicated AI core. This platform delivers 20× the AI throughput of prior generations, providing the necessary processing headroom for megapixel thermal AI detection.

Feature Capability
Thermal Resolution 1280×1024 imager
AI Throughput 20× increase over previous generations
TC12 Dual-Stream Processes 1280×1024 thermal and 4K visible streams simultaneously
On-Device Validation Real-time cross-validation between streams with no cloud dependency

On the TC12 model, the Gen7 platform runs independent AI models on both the thermal and visible streams simultaneously to cross-validate detections entirely on-device.

💡 Why it matters

The system is engineered to address the specific scale of critical infrastructure. “Critical infrastructure perimeters don’t fit in a small box. The NS12 and TC12 were built for exactly that challenge — protecting more perimeter with fewer devices, with the AI classification performance and trusted alerts that operators can rely on,” commented Jim Hahn, CEO, Sightlogix. The company indicates these products are the result of more than 20 years of engineering for this application.

#Sightlogix #ThermalImaging #PerimeterSecurity #EdgeAI #ComputerVision

Source: Sightlogix introduces new family of thermal cameras

item.title: Introduction of QVAC Genesis III STEM-Focused Synthetic Corpus
item.description:
Introduction of QVAC Genesis III STEM-Focused Synthetic Corpus

Researchers have introduced QVAC Genesis III, a multi-domain synthetic corpus designed to address the bottleneck of high-quality pre-training data for educational and STEM-specific language models targeting edge AI and on-device deployment.

🔍 Overview

QVAC Genesis III is a 191.43B-token corpus that covers 19 domains. It is designed to provide high per-token learning value for small models across several difficulty levels and different educational styles.

🧩 How it works

The corpus is built using a dual generation strategy that performs targeted teacher distillation using a weak edge-scale student model as a signal:

  • Student Failures: These are converted into corrective explanations.
  • Student Successes: These are expanded into contrastive option-level reasoning over all answer choices.

⚙️ Key details

To evaluate the data, a new LLM-as-a-parser protocol was introduced to track answer validity and extract final answers from free-form outputs. Validation was conducted via controlled from-scratch ablations using 1.7B-parameter models.

Benchmark Performance Result
ARC-E Up to +28.57% improvement
ARC-C Up to +21.35% improvement
Valid Answer Rate Up to 99.45%

💡 Why it matters

Models trained with QVAC Genesis III consistently outperform the publicly released Cosmo-1B model and those trained with the open-source synthetic corpus Cosmopedia-v2 across MMLU STEM, GPQA Diamond, and ARC benchmarks.

#STEM #SyntheticData #EdgeAI #LLM

Source: QVAC Genesis III: A Large-Scale, High-Quality Open Synthetic STEM Corpus for Efficient Language Model Pre-Training Source: Sample Count Is Not Enough: Candidate-Generation Strategy Shapes the Energy and Performance of LLM Test-Time Scaling Source: LSTM-UT and Recurrent-Depth Transformers on Cellular Automata Source: Learn Your Own Thoughts: Abstract Token Curriculum

item.title: NVIDIA TensorRT Edge-LLM Performance in MLPerf Inference v6.1 Edge Agentic Benchmark
item.description:
NVIDIA TensorRT Edge-LLM Performance in MLPerf Inference v6.1 Edge Agentic Benchmark

NVIDIA TensorRT Edge-LLM has completed the MLPerf Inference v6.1 Edge Agentic benchmark running the Qwen3.6-27B model on a single NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor Developer Kit.

⚙️ Key details

The system was configured with the following specifications:

  • Hardware: One NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor Developer Kit
  • Memory: 128 GB of unified memory
  • Power Mode: MAXN
  • Execution Mode: SingleStream
  • Model: Qwen3.6-27B

📊 Performance results

The TensorRT Edge-LLM submission completed the performance workload in 24 minutes and 36 seconds, which is 6.4x faster than the llama.cpp reference submission of 2 hours and 37 minutes.

Metric Value
Output throughput 52.33 tokens per second
Median time to first token 247.12 ms
Median time per output token 14.68 ms
BFCL overall accuracy 87.94%

🧩 How it works

The result was achieved using several optimization techniques:

  • Quantization: The submission used NVFP4 (a 4-bit floating-point format supported by the NVIDIA Blackwell GPU) for weights and activations, including the language-model head, and FP8 for the KV cache. This smaller representation increases available unified memory for application workloads, speculative decoding state, and long context.
  • KV Cache Reuse: TensorRT Edge-LLM identifies reusable prompt prefixes and restores cached attention KV pages. Because Qwen3.6 uses a hybrid model architecture, the runtime also restores partial KV-page state and the recurrent state. In this workload, approximately 96% of prompt tokens were served with hot cache, requiring the prefill of only ~0.5M of the 13.6M total prompt tokens.
  • Tree-based Multi-Token Prediction (MTP): A draft model predicts several future tokens which the target model verifies together in one forward pass. The server configuration utilized:
    • 8 draft steps
    • Top-2 candidates at each drafting depth
    • A 16-node verification tree

🔍 Overview

The MLPerf Edge Agentic benchmark measures OpenAI-compatible model endpoints across two phases:

  • Performance: The workload consists of 20 conversations and 1,007 generated turns. Input length grows to approximately 23.5K tokens.
  • Accuracy: This phase uses Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) v4 prompts with reasoning off and single-turn only to balance evaluation time and accuracy on edge devices.

#MLPerf #TensorRT #JetsonAGXThor #EdgeAI #LLM

Source: TensorRT Edge-LLM Completes the MLPerf Edge Agentic Benchmark 6.4x Faster on Jetson AGX Thor | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: Hefring Marine Selected for NATO DIANA Mission Track to Deploy Maritime AI
item.description:
Hefring Marine Selected for NATO DIANA Mission Track to Deploy Maritime AI

Icelandic tech company Hefring Marine has been selected as one of only 15 companies to advance to the Mission Track of NATO’s Defence Innovation Accelerator for the North Atlantic (DIANA). Chosen from a 2026 cohort of 150 innovators out of more than 3,600 proposals, Hefring Marine is the first and only Icelandic company to reach this stage of the programme, marking a major step toward deploying its maritime intelligence technology across NATO and Allied forces.

🔍 Overview

The Mission Track is the follow-on element of the DIANA programme, designed to support technologies that have demonstrated strong defense interest and alignment with Allied operational needs. Selected participants receive:

  • Up to €300,000 in non-dilutive funding
  • Continued access to NATO test centers
  • Tailored support to help transition technologies toward operational deployment

🧩 How it works

Hefring Marine’s solutions focus on connecting vessel data and providing real-time intelligence at sea:

Technology Description
ODIN (Observation and Domain Awareness Network) A maritime intelligence system designed to connect data from navigation and object-detection systems across existing vessels. It combines information across multiple platforms to provide a persistent, networked view of activity at sea to support intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) operations.
IMAS Hefring’s Marine Decision Intelligence platform, which uses edge AI to provide real-time decision support aboard crewed and uncrewed vessels. ODIN builds directly upon this technology.

⚙️ Key details

The selection follows a period of increasing collaboration between Hefring and Allied defense organizations:

  • Headquarters Demonstrations: In August, Hefring hosted NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe General Alexus G. Grynkewich, U.S. Permanent Representative to NATO Matthew Whitaker, and U.S. Ambassador to Iceland Billy Long at its Reykjavík headquarters for demonstrations of IMAS and ODIN. Hefring also recently welcomed Clara Ganslandt, Ambassador of the European Union to Iceland, to discuss the role of European maritime technology in safety and security.
  • Field Testing: Members of the Hefring team are currently participating in REPMUS 2026 in Portugal, an operational experimentation exercise for maritime robotics and uncrewed systems, allowing them to test and demonstrate the technology alongside potential end users.

💡 Why it matters

“Mission Track is important because with ODIN validated in real-time operations and exercises, the focus now moves decisively towards adoption,” said Karl Birgir Björnsson, CEO and co-founder of Hefring Marine. “Our priority now is to get these capabilities into the hands of operators, validate them in demanding environments and work through the practical steps needed to deploy them across existing Allied fleets. For a company that started in Reykjavík solving very practical problems aboard small vessels, the opportunity to contribute to maritime security at Alliance level is a significant milestone.”

item.title: Compact Open Models Bring Local Multi-Step Reasoning to NVIDIA Jetson Hardware
item.description:
Compact Open Models Bring Local Multi-Step Reasoning to NVIDIA Jetson Hardware

Until recently, models capable of multi-step reasoning were too large to run locally on edge hardware. Developers building agents have had to route inference through a data center, which added network dependency, increased costs, and exposed data that may need to stay on device.

Several model families released throughout the summer have collectively marked a turning point for edge AI. This new generation of compact open models now delivers reasoning and agentic capabilities that required large data center systems only a few months ago, and NVIDIA Jetson can run them today.

⚙️ Model Architecture and Target Workflows

These compact open models feature high-quality quantized checkpoints and optimized deployment options across popular inference engines. Developers can use Nemotron 3.5 Lightning and Qwen3.8-27B as examples of these different architectural approaches:

Model Architecture Total Parameters Active Parameters (Per Token) Best Fit Workflow
Nemotron 3.5 Lightning Mixture-of-experts (MoE) 30 billion 3 billion Response-heavy workflows, where faster token generation can shorten the overall process.
Qwen3.8-27B Dense 27 billion 27 billion Tasks that require fewer, harder decisions and allow the agent to spend more time generating each response.

Note: Distillation transfers some of Nemotron 3 Ultra’s capabilities into the smaller Nemotron 3.5 Lightning model.

🚀 Hardware and Deployment Options

Developers can deploy these models locally through popular frameworks, including vLLM and llama.cpp, ensuring the reasoning loop does not depend entirely on the data center. Deployment recommendations vary by hardware capability:

  • Jetson Orin Nano: Gemma 4 E4B is a strong starting point.
  • Jetson AGX Orin & Jetson AGX Thor: Nemotron 3.5 Lightning and Qwen3.8-27B are strong options.

🛠️ Performance Optimization Techniques

Two complementary techniques can be used to improve inference performance on Jetson hardware:

  • NVFP4 Quantization: Reduces the work and memory required for model operations. This format improves generation speed and reduces memory use while keeping quality close to BF16.
  • Speculative Decoding: A smaller draft model proposes several tokens, and the main model verifies them together. This process generates multiple accepted tokens per verification step.

These two optimizations complement each other: NVFP4 reduces the cost of each pass, while speculative decoding increases the number of accepted tokens produced from each pass. Combined, they improve performance.
